plot_extraction.response_text:
An aging businessman, Mr. Neave, walks home feeling suddenly exhausted and alienated from the springtime vitality around him. He worries that his spoiled, irresponsible son Harold cannot be trusted to inherit the successful business, despite his wife and daughters urging him to retire.

At home, his affluent family is absorbed in parties, clothes, and social gossip. Though they fuss over his tiredness, they barely attend to him as a person. While dressing for dinner, Mr. Neave dozes and envisions himself as a withered old man endlessly climbing stairs, compelled to return to the office because no one will stop or replace him. Awakening alone in the dark, he feels that his wife and children are strangers and that his life has passed him by. A memory of a loving young woman bidding him farewell makes him wonder whether his entire family life has been a mistake or a dream. When the servant announces dinner, he suppresses his distress and goes downstairs.

style_extraction.response_text:
The story uses a close third-person perspective that remains tightly aligned with old Mr. Neave’s consciousness. External narration repeatedly slips into free indirect discourse, allowing his habitual phrases—“H’m, h’m!”, “Well, well!”—and private judgments to colour the prose without formal transitions into thought. This creates an intimate yet slightly distanced psychological portrait: the reader inhabits his fatigue, resentment and bewilderment while also perceiving limitations that he cannot fully articulate. The narration becomes increasingly fluid as wakefulness gives way to drowsiness, memory and dream, mirroring his weakening grasp on his family and his own life.

The prose combines social realism with impressionistic and symbolic description. Concrete details establish an affluent urban household—carriages, fashionable streets, servants, tennis parties, expensive furnishings—but these surfaces are filtered through Mr. Neave’s altered perception. Spring is personified as a warm, eager young woman who threatens to drag him into its vitality, while the air seems to become “heavy and solid like water.” The family home, with its open windows, flowers and floating curtains, appears to announce the presence of “young life,” implicitly excluding its ageing provider. Such imagery transforms ordinary surroundings into emotional projections, so that physical objects and seasonal changes express exhaustion, alienation and mortality.

The style depends strongly on contrasts between brightness and darkness, youth and age, motion and stillness, abundance and depletion. The streets are full of golden light, clanking trams and hurrying crowds, whereas Mr. Neave feels cold, numb and unable to keep pace. Inside the house, his wife and daughters are vivid, noisy and socially animated, while he sinks into an immense chair and is gradually forgotten. Their world is “too rich for him,” a phrase that suggests not merely luxury but an oppressive excess of colour, sound, appetite and performance. By contrast, his inward world becomes dark, distant and attenuated.

Sentences vary according to emotional pressure. Long, cumulative sentences convey the crowded movement of the city, the expensive abundance of the household and the rambling associations of Mr. Neave’s mind. Short fragments, repetitions and exclamations register shocks of recognition: “Enjoying himself!”, “My treasure!”, “Stop him, stop him, somebody!” Ellipses frequently leave thoughts suspended or dissolving, suggesting fatigue, repression and incomplete understanding. Dashes and abrupt paragraph breaks likewise imitate the discontinuous movement between observation, remembered speech, fantasy and dream.

Dialogue is brisk, theatrical and socially revealing. Charlotte and the daughters speak in affectionate diminutives and exaggerated tones—crooning, wailing, coaxing, crying “tragically”—but their solicitude is shallow and self-absorbed. Their chatter about ices, dresses and dinner guests proceeds around Mr. Neave rather than engaging with him. Repeated endearments and playful reprimands disguise the extent to which they infantilise and disregard him. Marion’s voice is explicitly described as stage-like, reinforcing the sense that family life is a performance. Harold, meanwhile, is characterised largely through absence, reported behaviour and the reactions he inspires; his charm and irresponsibility dominate the story despite his minimal direct presence.

Repetition provides structural and psychological cohesion. Phrases such as “ideal family,” “enjoying himself,” “Where is Harold?” and “He said—” recur with increasingly ironic force. The label “ideal family” initially sounds like social praise but gradually exposes the gap between public appearance and emotional reality. Mr. Neave’s verbal tics convey an old-fashioned masculine reserve: instead of openly confronting disappointment or fear, he retreats into murmured formulas. The repeated unfinished reference to what Harold “said” also embodies evasion and deferred accountability.

A central symbolic figure is the “little ancient fellow” climbing endless stairs. At first Mr. Neave observes this figure as though it were someone else, but it is plainly a dissociated image of himself: frail, spider-like, condemned to move between office and home without belonging fully to either. The changing direction of his climb—from stairs to dining room, then toward the office—condenses his life into compulsive labour and exposes his inability to retire. This dreamlike double allows the prose to render an existential crisis indirectly rather than through explicit analysis.

The tone blends pathos, irony and muted social satire. Mr. Neave is treated sympathetically as an exhausted man who has sacrificed himself for a family that values his income more than his presence, yet he is not wholly idealised. His identity has been invested so completely in business and patriarchal provision that he has helped create the emotional distance he now discovers. The family’s polished sociability and material comfort are gently mocked, but the humour remains uneasy because it accompanies his dawning sense that his supposedly successful life may have been a mistake.

The closing movement becomes lyrical and uncanny. Temporal boundaries collapse as the present household turns strange and a fragmentary memory of a pale young woman emerges as his “real” wife, making the intervening years seem dreamlike. The passion-vine, mournful posture and whispered farewell give this memory a romantic, elegiac intensity absent from the family’s bright chatter. Yet the revelation is interrupted by the servant’s loud announcement that dinner is ready. Mr. Neave’s final response—“I’m coming, I’m coming”—is ordinary but ambiguous: it signals his return to domestic ritual while also faintly suggesting surrender, ageing and an approach toward death.

### The House in Spring

At six o’clock Mr. Neave left the office.

For several minutes he stood beneath the stone archway, one gloved hand resting on the brass rail, while the city hurried past as though it had received astonishing news. The trams clanged; wheels flashed; young men sprang on and off the steps of omnibuses; girls in pale dresses streamed from the shops with parcels balanced against their hips. Above the roofs the sky was still golden, and every upper window held a square of fire.

Spring! It had come in a single afternoon, warm, scented, importunate. It pressed against him like an eager young creature crying, “Come along! Quickly! You mustn’t miss it!”

But Mr. Neave did not want to be touched by spring.

He was cold. Cold and tired—absurdly tired. His knees trembled beneath his weight, and his fingers, gripping the rail, seemed hardly to belong to him.

H’m, h’m! This was unusual.

He had walked home every fine evening for thirty-seven years. It was one of his rules. A man who sat at a desk all day needed exercise. He had said so a thousand times, especially to Harold, who believed exercise meant driving to the tennis club and strolling twice round the lawns.

Yet the long shining street before him appeared impossible. The air had thickened. It was no longer air at all, but warm transparent water through which he must push his old body while the young darted past like bright fish.

Old body? Nonsense.

He descended the steps carefully.

At the corner a flower seller held out bunches of violets. Their sweetness reached him with almost painful sharpness. For one moment he thought of buying some for Charlotte. But Charlotte’s rooms were already full of flowers. There would be bowls in the drawing room, jars on the stairs, perhaps lilies at dinner. Flowers arrived constantly: from the girls’ admirers, from hostesses, from Harold when he remembered he had forgotten something.

Harold.

The name seemed to weigh more heavily than his coat.

That morning Mr. Neave had again found the correspondence unopened on Harold’s desk. Three letters from Melbourne, two telegrams, and the revised contract lying where it had been put yesterday. Harold had appeared at noon, beautifully dressed and faintly apologetic.

“My dear governor, don’t look like that. I was kept up horribly late.”

Kept up! At the Bellmans’ supper, no doubt, or playing cards with those fellows at the club. Enjoying himself.

And when Mr. Neave had spoken—quietly, reasonably—of responsibility, Harold had smiled and said—

Well, what had he said?

Something about not letting business become a disease. Something light, clever, intolerable.

“He’ll settle down,” Charlotte always declared. “You never give the boy time.”

Time! Harold was thirty-one.

Mr. Neave moved with the crowd, though more than once a shoulder struck his arm and someone turned impatiently. He wished they would not hurry so. What could be waiting for them? Dinners, theatres, women at lighted windows. Young life calling to young life.

The thought came oddly: there was no call for him.

At home, however, they were always begging him to retire.

“You’ve earned your rest, Father,” the girls cried.

Charlotte said it tenderly, almost proudly. “We can’t have you wearing yourself out. Harold will manage splendidly.”

Splendidly! H’m, h’m!

They knew nothing of the business. They saw the car at the door, the summer house, the servants, the accounts paid without question. They had never watched a doubtful investment through sleepless months or sat opposite a ruined man who still smiled while signing his name. To them the business was a deep, dependable well. Harold need only lean over and lower the bucket.

But suppose the rope slipped?

At the next crossing Mr. Neave paused so long that a policeman touched his sleeve.

“Now then, sir.”

“Yes, yes. Quite.”

He reached the quieter streets at last. The gardens there were overflowing. Branches of blossom hung above white walls; lawns shone with new grass; curtains breathed from open windows. The houses looked freshly awakened, their bright faces turned toward evening.

His own house stood at the end of the crescent, wide and creamy, with green shutters and a balcony tangled in young vine. All the windows were open. A long curtain floated outward and fell back, floated and fell, as though the house itself were breathing.

On the steps stood two tennis racquets, a silver-headed cane and a basket of pink roses.

How full it was. Full of flowers, clothes, visitors, music, laughter. Full of everything he had laboured to give them.

And yet, approaching it, Mr. Neave felt like a tradesman arriving at the wrong door.

The maid opened before he rang.

“Mrs. Neave and the young ladies are in the morning room, sir.”

From somewhere within came Marion’s voice, high and tragic.

“But, Mother, if she wears yellow I shall simply refuse to go!”

Then laughter—Charlotte’s soft peal, Ethel’s sharper one—and the faint clatter of teacups.

Mr. Neave removed his hat. The hall, crowded with palms and polished tables, swayed slightly.

“There he is!” cried Ethel.

They came at once, all three of them, wonderfully fresh and finished. Charlotte wore grey silk with a fall of lace; Ethel was in white; Marion had a green ribbon about her dark hair. They surrounded him in a cloud of perfume.

“Father, how dreadful you look!”

“My poor old darling!”

“Sit down instantly.”

Charlotte took his hand between hers. “You’re frozen.”

“No, no. Merely a little tired.”

“A little!” Marion repeated, as if before an audience. “He admits to being a little tired. Mother, ring for brandy. Ring for a doctor. Ring for the archbishop!”

They guided him into the morning room and lowered him into the largest chair. Cushions were pushed behind his head; a footstool appeared; someone loosened his collar.

This was kindness, certainly. An ideal family, people called them. The Neaves—so united, so affectionate. He ought to feel grateful.

But they had already turned away.

“Where were we?” Ethel asked.

“Clara’s dress.”

“Yellow,” Marion said darkly.

Charlotte poured tea while the girls discussed Clara, who had become engaged to a man none of them admired but all of them intended to dine with on Thursday. There were ices to be ordered for Saturday, a garden party on Monday, and the question of whether Mrs. Bellman had deliberately failed to invite the Ashfords.

Their voices flew over Mr. Neave like ribbons in a wind.

He looked at the laden table: little cakes glazed in pink and green, strawberries under silver, thin bread, cream, honey, two kinds of jam. Too much. The room itself was too much—too soft, too bright, too sweet. Roses leaned from painted bowls; the carpet glowed beneath his shoes; tiny gilt chairs stood about waiting for tiny gilt people.

It was all too rich for him.

“Where is Harold?” he asked.

Nobody heard.

Marion was imitating Mrs. Bellman: one hand upon her heart, her eyes lifted.

“My dear, happiness has made you positively plain!”

They screamed with laughter.

“Where is Harold?” Mr. Neave repeated.

Charlotte glanced round. “Harold? He telephoned, darling. He may be late.”

“Late for dinner?”

“He said—what did he say, Ethel?”

“Oh, something about Tom Fraser and a horse.”

“No, it was the motor.”

“He said,” Charlotte began, smiling vaguely, “he said not to wait if—”

The three of them looked at one another.

“Well, it doesn’t matter,” she concluded. “He is enjoying himself.”

Enjoying himself.

Mr. Neave closed his eyes. Instantly the colours of the room burned brighter behind his lids.

“Father’s falling asleep,” Ethel whispered.

“Let him. He looks worn out.”

“Poor treasure.”

Their voices softened for perhaps half a minute. Then Marion remembered the blue sash, and the talk sprang up again.

After a while Charlotte rang. William came to help Mr. Neave upstairs.

“I can manage,” he said.

Of course he could manage. He mounted slowly, refusing the arm held near his elbow. At each landing he paused as if examining the pictures. Family portraits, landscapes, horses—the things one put upon stairs because nobody looked at them.

His room was cool and shadowy. The sun had withdrawn from that side of the house, and the open window admitted a smell of damp earth. William laid out his dinner clothes and departed.

Mr. Neave sat before the dressing table.

There he was in the glass: a heavy old face, grey moustache, pale folds beneath the eyes. Not ill. No. But changed. He leaned closer.

When had that happened?

He remembered his father at sixty-eight, stern and broad in a black coat, already an old man. But Mr. Neave himself was sixty-eight. Curious. All his life old age had remained his father’s possession, an ugly coat hanging in another man’s cupboard. Now, somehow, he had put it on.

Well, well!

He began to undress. One boot came off. The other resisted, and the effort left him breathless. He rested his head against the chair.

Only for a moment.

From far below came a doorbell, quick footsteps, a burst of greeting. The house trembled with arrivals. Or perhaps it was not the house. Perhaps it was the street, the whole city, vibrating with youth and spring.

Mr. Neave saw a staircase.

It rose steeply through darkness, step upon step, without banister or landing. A little ancient fellow was climbing it. His coat hung from his shoulders; his thin legs bent like wire; one hand clutched a bundle of papers to his chest.

Painfully he lifted one foot, then the other.

Who was the fellow? Some clerk kept too long? Someone Mr. Neave ought to pension?

“Stop him,” Mr. Neave tried to say. “That’s enough. Tell him to come down.”

But the climber went on.

At the top was the dining room, brilliant with candles. Charlotte and the girls sat among silver and flowers, laughing. A chair waited at the end of the table.

The old fellow climbed toward it.

No—he had turned. Now the staircase led to the office. Desks floated above him; ledgers opened their great black wings; telephones rang from step to step.

He must get back. There was no one else. Harold had not come. Harold had said—

What had Harold said?

The ancient fellow stumbled, caught himself, climbed again.

“Stop him, somebody!”

But the family only laughed. Their mouths opened and closed soundlessly. Charlotte raised a glass. Marion wore yellow now, or was it flame? Ethel’s pearls ran like drops of water down her dress.

The little fellow was Mr. Neave.

He knew this without surprise. He was watching himself climb and was also inside that trembling body, feeling each step strike upward through his bones. The papers beneath his arm grew heavier. Contracts, mortgages, bills, invitations, dressmakers’ accounts, school fees, jewellery, journeys, flowers—everything the house had eaten, everything it still demanded.

At the top Harold lounged in Mr. Neave’s chair, young, handsome, smiling.

“My dear governor,” he said, “why do you take things so seriously?”

Then the chair was empty.

The stairs continued.

Mr. Neave woke.

The room was dark.

For a time he did not move. He could hear music downstairs—a piano touched lightly, then laughter. They had not called him. Or they had called and he had not answered. His shirt lay across his knees, and one foot was still booted.

Outside, the last light had gone from the sky. The window was a black square in which one pale curtain stirred.

He did not know where he was.

That was his bed, surely; those were his brushes, his watch, Charlotte’s photograph in the silver frame. Yet each object appeared to belong to a room prepared for him by strangers. Even the photograph was strange. Charlotte smiled beneath a broad hat, charming and composed. His wife. Yes.

But what did that mean?

Downstairs were his daughters, women with smooth arms and bright voices. Harold, wherever he might be, was his son. They possessed his name, his house, the years of his labour. Still, he could not reach them. There was a clear hard wall between them and him, like glass in the dark.

Had he loved them? Certainly. He had provided, protected, arranged. He had hurried from breakfast to office, office to dinner, winter to summer, one year into the next. He had signed cheques, approved schools, bought horses, taken houses by the sea. Love had been included in all that. Naturally.

But where had his life gone while he was arranging theirs?

A woman’s face appeared before him.

Not Charlotte’s.

A pale young face under a garden hat; dark eyes wet with grief. Behind her, leaves of a passion-vine clung to a veranda post, and purple flowers hung like little wounded hearts. She held both his hands.

“You will forget,” she whispered.

He could almost hear the insects humming in the hot garden. He could smell dust and crushed mint beneath their feet. He had been young—astonishingly young—and she had loved him. Or he had loved her. There had been a farewell, a journey, a promise he had not kept.

What was her name?

He bent toward her in memory, but the years rushed between them: the wedding, the first office, Charlotte’s parties, babies, illnesses, accounts, Harold’s school reports, larger premises, a larger house. The pale girl withdrew behind it all, still watching him.

My true wife, he thought wildly. My lost life.

Then which life had been the dream? This house, this family, this endless prosperous day? Had he fallen asleep in that far garden and imagined thirty-seven years of work? Or had he dreamed the girl because the darkness required one person who had once seen him—not the provider, not the governor, not poor old Father, but himself?

He lifted his hands. They were old hands.

From below came a tremendous burst of laughter. The chandelier must be lighted now. Charlotte would be at the head of the table, Ethel beside some young man, Marion performing her despair. Harold’s chair might still be empty.

An ideal family.

Mr. Neave smiled, though his mouth trembled.

A knock sounded, and William entered with quiet disapproval.

“Dinner is served, sir. Mrs. Neave asked me to say they are waiting.”

Waiting. At last they were waiting for him.

The servant switched on the light. The pale girl vanished. The staircase became only the familiar carpeted passage beyond the door.

Mr. Neave looked at his unfinished dressing, at the stubborn boot, at his face startled in the mirror. For one instant he wanted to cry out—to tell William that there had been some mistake, that the years were wrong, that another life was hidden just behind this one.

Instead he straightened his shoulders.

“Yes, yes,” he said. “I’m coming.”

William withdrew.

Mr. Neave rose carefully. From downstairs came the bright clink of silver, and Charlotte’s voice floated upward, affectionate, impatient:

“Where is he?”

“I’m coming,” he called again.

And, gripping the banister, he began to descend.

# The Hour That Went Missing

At 2:17 every morning, the clocks in Bellwether stopped.

They did not slow down or lose their rhythm one tick at a time. They simply ceased. Pendulums hung motionless. Gears held their breath. Even the great clock in the courthouse tower, whose iron hands weighed more than a grown man, froze at seventeen minutes past two.

Then, at 3:17, all the clocks began again.

No one in Bellwether remembered when the missing hour had first disappeared. Most people had learned to ignore it. Bakers set their alarms early. Nurses adjusted their rounds. The railway added sixty minutes to every overnight journey through town. Visitors complained, but locals merely shrugged.

“An old electrical fault,” said the mayor, although many clocks required no electricity.

“Something in the water,” said the doctor, though no one could explain why water would stop a pocket watch.

“Mountains,” said people who preferred an answer that sounded natural and required no further thought.

Only Elias Vale, the town clockmaker, considered the missing hour an insult.

His shop stood in a narrow lane behind the courthouse. Hundreds of clocks covered its walls: brass carriage clocks, painted cuckoo clocks, walnut mantel clocks, silver watches, and tiny travel clocks with luminous hands. Their combined ticking sounded like summer rain.

At 2:17 each morning, Elias sat among them and listened to the silence.

He was seventy-three years old, lean as a clock hand, with silver hair and a magnifying lens that seemed permanently fixed over his right eye. He had lived alone since his wife, Mara, vanished nineteen years earlier.

People said she had left him. There had been no body, no note, no sign of struggle. Her coat and shoes were gone, and so was the small blue suitcase she used when visiting her sister.

But Elias knew Mara had not left.

She had disappeared at 2:17 in the morning.

He had woken to find her side of the bed empty. Downstairs, the front door stood open. Snow blew across the floorboards. Her footprints led from the house into the white street and ended beneath the courthouse clock, as if she had been lifted straight into the sky.

At 3:17, the clocks began ticking again, and Elias discovered that an hour had passed.

From that night onward, he stayed awake during the silence.

For nineteen years, nothing happened.

Then, on the first morning of winter, someone knocked on his shop door at 2:43.

Elias was so startled that he dropped his tea.

The knock came again: three slow taps.

None of the clocks moved. Outside, snow hung frozen in the air. Through the window, Elias could see individual flakes suspended above the street like stars trapped in glass.

He approached the door.

“Who is it?”

No one answered.

He opened it.

A girl stood on the threshold. She looked about twelve years old and wore a red wool coat several sizes too large. Her dark hair was tied with a yellow ribbon. Under one arm, she carried a wooden clock shaped like a house.

“Are you Elias Vale?” she asked.

“I am.”

“You took long enough.”

She pushed past him into the shop.

Elias stared at the motionless snow, then shut the door. “Who are you?”

“June.”

“June what?”

“Just June.”

She placed the wooden clock on his workbench. It was beautifully made, with carved windows and a tiny green door. Instead of numbers, its face displayed painted images: a candle, a key, a bird, a boat, a tree, a crown, and other symbols Elias did not recognize. It had only one hand, and that hand pointed nowhere.

“It’s broken,” June said.

“All clocks are broken when they come to me.”

“Not like this one.”

Elias examined it. The casing had no screws, seams, or hinges. He pressed his ear to the wood and heard a faint rushing sound, like distant wind.

“Where did you get it?”

“My mother gave it to me.”

“And where is she?”

June looked toward the courthouse tower visible through the window.

“She’s in the hour.”

Elias’s hands became cold.

“What hour?”

“The one your town lost.”

He lowered himself onto his stool. “That is not an answer a child should give lightly.”

“I’m not a child.”

“You look like one.”

“You look like an old man. Appearances can be accurate without being complete.”

Despite himself, Elias almost smiled. It was the sort of answer Mara would have enjoyed.

He lifted the clock. Though no larger than a breadbox, it was surprisingly heavy.

“How do I open it?”

“With the key.”

“And where is the key?”

“In the clock.”

“That is inconvenient.”

“It’s a clock made from time,” June said. “Convenience wasn’t the point.”

Before Elias could ask what she meant, the wooden clock shuddered. Its single hand swung toward the painted bird.

A cuckoo door opened above its face.

Instead of a mechanical bird, a folded strip of paper slid out.

Elias unfolded it.

In Mara’s handwriting were four words:

Please come before dawn.

He sat perfectly still.

June watched him. “You know her writing.”

“Where did you get this?”

“I told you. The clock.”

“Do not play games with me.”

“I don’t have time for games.”

“No one does, apparently.”

June sighed and climbed onto the stool opposite him.

“Long ago,” she said, “before Bellwether was built, there was a keeper beneath the hill. He looked after unwanted time.”

“Unwanted time?”

“Moments people wished away. Long winters. Sleepless nights. Final goodbyes. The minute before bad news. All the time people begged to escape had to go somewhere.”

“And it went beneath the hill?”

“Yes. The keeper stored it in a great clock. For centuries, that was enough. Then people made more clocks, more schedules, more deadlines. They began wishing away nearly everything. Workdays. Rainy afternoons. Years of loneliness. Childhoods they wanted to outgrow. Old age they feared enduring.”

Elias glanced at the frozen clocks surrounding them.

“The great clock filled up,” June continued. “So the keeper stole an hour from Bellwether. It was supposed to be temporary, just enough room to repair the mechanism. But something went wrong. The keeper disappeared, and the stolen hour became a cage.”

“For Mara?”

“For everyone who entered it.”

Elias gripped the note. “Why would she enter?”

“To find the keeper.”

“She knew about this?”

“Some people do. Your wife was curious.”

“That is one word for it.”

“She believed she could restore the hour.”

Elias looked again at the message. “And you say she is your mother.”

June nodded.

“Mara and I had no children.”

“Not before she vanished.”

The room seemed to tilt.

Elias rose so quickly that his stool fell backward. “Enough.”

June did not move.

“You expect me to believe my wife entered a hidden hour, remained there for nineteen years, and had a daughter?”

“Time behaves differently inside itself.”

“That sentence means nothing.”

“It will.”

At that moment, the green door on the wooden clock opened. A brass key dropped onto the workbench.

June picked it up.

“You can stay here if you like,” she said. “At 3:17, I’ll disappear, the clock will close, and the missing hour will continue forever. Your wife will wait. You’ll sit among your clocks for however many years you have left.”

Elias stared at the key.

“What happens if I come?”

“You may not return.”

“Will Mara?”

“I don’t know.”

He took his coat from its hook.

“Then let us not waste time.”

Outside, Bellwether lay silent and motionless. Snowflakes remained suspended above rooftops. A cat hung in mid-leap between two barrels. Smoke stood above chimneys in pale, unmoving pillars.

June carried the wooden clock. Elias followed her across the square.

At the courthouse, she knelt beside the tower’s stone foundation. Near the ground was a carving Elias had passed thousands of times without noticing: a circle containing a candle, a key, a bird, and a crown.

June pressed the brass key into the carving.

Stone softened around it.

A narrow door appeared.

Beyond it, steps descended into darkness.

Elias took a lantern from his coat pocket, lit it, and followed June underground. The door closed behind them with a sound like a clock case snapping shut.

The staircase went deeper than the hill should have allowed. Its walls were covered with messages scratched into the stone.

Not yet.

I need more time.

Let this day end.

Take me back.

At the bottom, they entered a vast cavern.

Thousands of glass spheres floated in the darkness. Some were no larger than marbles; others were broad as houses. Within each sphere, a moment repeated.

A soldier embraced his mother beside a train.

A woman sat alone at a birthday table, watching candles burn down.

A child waited outside a headmaster’s office.

A fisherman struggled through a storm.

A bride stood before a mirror, unable to lift her veil.

Elias moved closer to one sphere. Inside, a younger version of himself sat beside Mara on a riverbank. She was laughing because he had dropped their picnic basket in the water.

“That was forty-seven years ago,” he whispered.

“Someone wished the afternoon would never end,” June said.

“I did.”

“Then part of it came here.”

Elias watched his younger self retrieve an apple from the river while Mara laughed so hard she had to hold his shoulder.

He wanted to touch the glass.

June caught his hand. “Don’t. Memories are greedy.”

They continued.

The cavern narrowed into a corridor filled with doors. Behind each came a different sound: thunder, music, weeping, applause, the crash of waves.

At the corridor’s end stood a clock tall as the courthouse tower.

Its gears filled the chamber. Copper wheels turned slowly through stone. Chains vanished into the ceiling. The pendulum, a black blade, hung motionless above a bottomless pit.

The clock face bore the same symbols as the wooden clock.

At its base, a woman in a gray dress worked among the gears.

Her hair, once black, was threaded with silver. She held a wrench in one hand. There was grease on her cheek.

Elias knew her at once.

“Mara.”

She turned.

For a moment, she looked exactly as she had on the night she vanished: alert, impatient, and already thinking three thoughts ahead. Then the wrench fell from her hand.

“Elias?”

He crossed the chamber without remembering the steps between them.

She met him halfway.

For nineteen years, Elias had imagined what he would say if he found her. He had prepared accusations, questions, declarations, and speeches polished by loneliness.

He said none of them.

He held her.

Mara pressed her face against his coat. He felt her shoulders shake.

“You got old,” she murmured.

“You did not have the decency to wait for me.”

She laughed, and the sound was so familiar that grief struck him harder than joy.

When they separated, Mara saw June.

“You found him.”

“He needed convincing,” June said.

“He always does.”

Elias looked from one to the other. “She says she is your daughter.”

“Our daughter,” Mara replied.

Elias felt the words enter him slowly.

“How?”

“On my first night here, I found a room full of possible tomorrows. In one of them, you and I had a child. A girl with my stubbornness and your habit of taking things apart.”

“I do not take things apart without reason.”

June raised an eyebrow.

Mara smiled faintly. “The missing hour makes possibilities solid. June was only an unlived future at first, but she grew. I taught her. She helped me.”

“Am I real?” June asked. Her tone was casual, but her hands tightened around the wooden clock.

Elias looked at her red coat, her yellow ribbon, and the challenging set of her mouth.

He thought of all the questions that could not be repaired by logic.

“You are here,” he said. “That is usually enough.”

June looked down quickly.

A deep metallic groan passed through the chamber.

One of the giant clock’s gears cracked. Black dust poured from its teeth.

Mara snatched up her wrench. “We have little time.”

“I was told that was our principal resource,” Elias said.

“Not anymore.”

She led him to the clock’s base. Behind a panel lay a tangled mechanism. Most of it was impossibly old, made from dark metal and bone-white ivory. At its center was a small, empty space shaped like a heart.

“The mainspring shattered,” Mara said. “The keeper tried to replace it with the stolen hour, but the hour had too many moments inside it. Too much regret. The mechanism jammed.”

“Where is the keeper?”

She pointed upward.

Entangled in the clock’s gears was a figure in a long black coat. His body had become part of the machine. Brass roots ran through his arms. His open eyes moved with every turn of a wheel.

“He has been holding the clock together,” Mara said. “If it breaks, all the unwanted time will return at once.”

“What would that mean?”

“Everyone would relive every moment they ever wished away. All at the same time.”

Elias considered the mechanism. “You have spent nineteen years repairing this?”

“Three years, from my perspective.”

“That is still a long time to leave your husband uninformed.”

“I sent notes.”

“I received one.”

“I sent four hundred.”

“Postal service has declined.”

Another crack split a gear overhead.

The keeper opened his mouth, and the entire clock spoke with him.

“A HEART,” it boomed.

Elias stepped back.

“A HEART MUST BE GIVEN.”

Mara gripped his arm. “That is the only repair I could not make.”

“What does it mean?”

“The clock needs a living heart to measure living time.”

June set the wooden clock on the floor. “Mine.”

“No,” Mara said immediately.

“I was made here. I’m part of the hour.”

“No.”

“If I take the keeper’s place, the mechanism will work.”

“You do not know that.”

“I do.”

Elias studied the heart-shaped space inside the clock.

“You said a living heart,” he murmured. “Not a life.”

Mara recognized the tone in his voice. “What are you thinking?”

“Every clock has an escapement. It does not create power. It controls its release.”

“This is not one of your mantel clocks.”

“No. It is badly designed.”

The keeper’s eyes shifted toward him, perhaps in offense.

Elias removed his pocket watch.

It was a plain silver watch, scratched along the case. Mara had given it to him on their tenth wedding anniversary. He had carried it every day since.

At 2:17 each morning, it stopped with the others.

Elias opened the back.

Inside the lid, Mara had once engraved a line:

All my hours are yours.

He showed it to her.

“A heart is not only an organ,” he said. “Sometimes it is the thing that carries what the heart cannot.”

Mara shook her head. “Sentiment will not repair a cosmic mechanism.”

“You married a clockmaker. Show some faith in precision.”

He placed the pocket watch into the empty space.

Nothing happened.

June looked disappointed.

Then Elias reached into the mechanism and turned the winding crown.

Once.

Twice.

On the third turn, the watch began to tick.

The sound echoed through the chamber.

The great clock answered.

One gear moved, then another. Chains drew tight. The black pendulum swung over the pit.

The keeper screamed.

Brass roots tore from his arms. He fell from the machinery, but instead of striking the floor, he broke apart into thousands of moths that flew upward and vanished.

The glass spheres throughout the cavern began to burst.

Released moments rushed through the chamber: rain, laughter, gunfire, lullabies, farewells, bells, and whispered names. They spiraled around the great clock, becoming a bright river.

The single hand on its face moved from the painted bird toward the painted tree.

Mara grabbed Elias.

“What have you done?”

“Repaired it, I hope.”

“The hour is restarting. We have to leave.”

They ran.

The corridor doors flew open as they passed. Storms and songs spilled after them. In the cavern, the floating memories shattered one by one.

Elias saw the riverbank again. His younger self and Mara sat in the grass beneath a golden afternoon.

For one dangerous second, he wanted to remain.

Then the memory-Mara turned toward him. Though she should not have been able to see beyond her moment, she smiled.

Go, her lips seemed to say.

Elias ran on.

They reached the stairs as the underground clock struck three.

The sound shook dust from the walls.

June unlocked the stone door. White light poured through.

They stumbled into the square.

Behind them, the entrance vanished.

For a breath, Bellwether remained frozen.

Then every suspended snowflake fell at once.

The cat landed between the barrels. Smoke curled above the chimneys. The courthouse clock groaned and moved forward.

Its minute hand passed 2:17.

Elias, Mara, and June stood beneath the tower, watching.

2:18.

From houses across town came shouts. Lights appeared in windows. Somewhere, a baby began to cry. Somewhere else, a man laughed.

The missing hour had returned.

Mara took Elias’s hand. “What happens now?”

He looked at her, then at June.

For years, he had imagined the restoration of his old life: Mara coming home, the dust of loneliness swept away, every interrupted plan resumed.

But time did not repair by moving backward.

It repaired by continuing.

“We open the shop late,” he said. “Then we have breakfast.”

June frowned. “That’s all?”

“No. After breakfast, your mother will explain four hundred undelivered notes. Then you will tell me how old you actually are. Then we will find you a coat that fits.”

“I like this coat.”

“It is absurd.”

“It has pockets.”

“So do sensible coats.”

Mara slipped her arm through his. “You see? She is ours.”

They crossed the square together.

Behind them, the courthouse clock struck the quarter hour. All over Bellwether, clocks answered—some early, some late, none quite agreeing, but all moving.

In the shop, Elias found that most of his clocks had survived. A few had lost a minute. One ran backward. The blue cuckoo clock insisted it was Thursday, although it was Monday.

On his workbench stood the wooden clock shaped like a house.

Its painted symbols were gone.

In their place were twelve ordinary numbers and three black hands.

The tiny green door opened.

Elias waited for a note, a key, or some new impossibility.

Instead, a wooden bird emerged and gave a single, cheerful call.

June laughed.

Mara leaned against Elias’s shoulder.

Outside, dawn approached, slow and pale beyond the roofs. The town had sixty new minutes and no idea what to do with them.

Elias listened to the clocks ticking around his family.

For the first time in nineteen years, the sound did not remind him of something being lost.

It sounded like something being given.
